heading: Minnesota Paycheck Calculator

parts.markdown:
Use our free **Minnesota paycheck calculator** to estimate your take-home pay after federal income tax, Minnesota income tax, Social Security, Medicare and applicable Minnesota Paid Leave contributions.

Enter your annual salary or hourly wage, choose your payment frequency and customize your withholding information to understand how much money you could receive on payday.

Minnesota uses progressive state income tax rates and introduced a new paid family and medical leave program in January 2026. These requirements make it important to use current payroll calculations when estimating your net earnings.

Whether you work in Minneapolis, Saint Paul, Rochester, Duluth or another Minnesota community, this calculator can help you compare employment opportunities and manage your monthly expenses.

## How to Use the Minnesota Paycheck Calculator

Begin by selecting annual salary or hourly wages.

Enter your gross earnings before taxes and deductions. Hourly employees should include their regular hours and qualifying overtime hours.

Select your payment frequency. Enter the federal and Minnesota income tax withheld for the pay period from your pay stub.

Include retirement contributions and healthcare premiums. If Minnesota Paid Leave was withheld, enter the amount under Benefits in Advanced settings, under Other deductions.

Enter prior year-to-date taxable wages if you are approaching a Social Security or Additional Medicare threshold.

Review your estimated federal withholding, Minnesota income tax, payroll contributions and remaining take-home pay.

For greater accuracy, use information from your latest pay stub and withholding certificates.

Your actual deductions depend on taxable earnings, withholding elections, employee benefits and employment circumstances.

The [Minnesota Department of Revenue](https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/) publishes official state income tax and withholding information.

## How Minnesota Income Tax Withholding Works

Minnesota applies a progressive individual income tax system.

Its 2026 automated payroll withholding method uses four marginal tax rates: 5.35%, 6.80%, 7.85% and 9.85%.

Employers calculate withholding by annualizing taxable wages, subtracting the value of applicable withholding allowances, applying the appropriate percentage schedule and converting the result back to the relevant payroll period.

For 2026, each ordinary Minnesota withholding allowance has an annual value of $5,300.

This amount reduces the wages used in the withholding calculation. It is not an additional cash payment or a direct tax credit.

The [2026 Minnesota Withholding Tax Instructions and Tables](https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/sites/default/files/2025-12/wh-inst-26.pdf) provide the complete employer calculation methodology.

## Minnesota Withholding Percentage Schedules

The following thresholds apply to the 2026 automated withholding formula after subtracting applicable allowances.

### Single withholding classification

These are adjusted-wage payroll withholding thresholds rather than the ordinary income tax brackets used on Minnesota annual tax returns.

Employers must also apply the appropriate base tax amounts from the official computer formula.

## Minnesota Income Tax Withholding Example

Suppose an employee receives $2,500 biweekly in Minnesota taxable wages, uses the single withholding classification and claims one ordinary withholding allowance.

Annualized wages:

$2,500 × 26 = $65,000

Subtract the applicable withholding allowance:

$65,000 − $5,300 = $59,700

The adjusted wages fall into the applicable 6.80% withholding bracket.

Using the official base amount of $1,782.09 and the lower bracket threshold of $38,010:

Annualized withholding:

$1,782.09 + (($59,700 − $38,010) × 0.068)

Annualized withholding equals $3,257.01.

Biweekly withholding:

$3,257.01 ÷ 26 = approximately $125.27

An employer using the permitted whole-dollar rounding method may withhold $125 instead.

Your actual withholding may differ if you claim additional allowances, request extra withholding or have deductions affecting taxable wages.

## Understanding Minnesota Form W-4MN

Minnesota employees generally provide withholding information using Form W-4MN.

This certificate allows employees to communicate their state withholding allowances and additional withholding requests to employers.

The modern federal Form W-4 does not use the same allowance-based structure. Consequently, federal withholding elections should not automatically be copied onto Form W-4MN.

For a new employee who has not provided Form W-4MN before the first wage payment, ordinary withholding generally defaults to the single classification with zero allowances.

Employees should review their withholding information after employment changes or significant changes in household circumstances.

Read the official [Minnesota Form W-4MN guidance](https://www.revenue.state.mn.us/form-w-4mn) for additional instructions.

## Minnesota Paid Leave Contributions in 2026

Minnesota's Paid Leave program became operational on January 1, 2026.

The program provides eligible workers with partial income replacement and employment protections during qualifying periods of family or medical leave.

For 2026, the standard combined employer and employee contribution rate is 0.88%.

Employers may generally deduct up to 0.44% from covered employee wages.

Certain qualifying small employers have reduced overall premium obligations. However, the employee contribution is still subject to the applicable maximum.

Employers may also choose to pay more than their required share, reducing the amount deducted from employee earnings.

Minnesota uses a rounded annual contribution ceiling of $185,000 for 2026.

At the full 0.44% employee rate, the maximum standard annual contribution is $814.

Visit the official [Minnesota Paid Leave website](https://paidleave.mn.gov/) for current program information.

## Federal Taxes Deducted From Minnesota Paychecks

Federal income tax withholding depends on taxable earnings, filing status, pay frequency and information supplied on Form W-4.

Social Security generally applies at 6.2% of covered wages, subject to the 2026 annual wage ceiling of $184,500.

Ordinary Medicare withholding applies at 1.45% of covered earnings without a standard annual wage ceiling.

Employers generally withhold an additional 0.9% when Medicare-covered wages paid by that employer exceed $200,000 during the calendar year.

The Minnesota Paid Leave contribution has a separate rounded wage ceiling and should not be confused with the federal Social Security limit.

Review [IRS Publication 15-T](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15t) and the [IRS Employer's Tax Guide](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15) for official federal payroll requirements.

## Minnesota Paycheck Example: $65,000 Salary

Consider an employee earning $65,000 annually and receiving 26 biweekly paychecks.

Assume the employee uses the single Minnesota withholding classification, claims one state withholding allowance and has no additional benefit deductions.

For federal withholding, assume a single employee with a modern Form W-4, no multiple-jobs adjustment and no additional credits or withholding.

This example assumes all earnings are covered by ordinary payroll contributions, the maximum standard employee paid leave rate applies and no annual wage thresholds have been reached.

Actual payroll results may differ because of withholding elections, employer contributions and rounding procedures.

## Minnesota Hourly Paycheck Calculator

Hourly workers can estimate earnings using their hourly wage and regular working hours, together with qualifying overtime compensation.

Suppose an employee earns $29 per hour and works 40 regular hours plus six qualifying overtime hours at time-and-a-half.

Regular earnings:

$29 × 40 = $1,160

Overtime earnings:

$29 × 1.5 × 6 = $261

Total gross earnings:

$1,421

Federal income tax, Minnesota income tax and applicable payroll contributions are then calculated using their respective taxable wage amounts.

Minnesota and federal overtime requirements can differ depending on the employee's coverage and employment classification.

Consult the [Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry overtime guidance](https://www.dli.mn.gov/business/employment-practices/overtime-laws) before estimating compensation for specialized employment arrangements.

## Working Across Minnesota State Borders

Minnesota has reciprocal income tax agreements with Michigan and North Dakota covering qualifying employee compensation.

Eligible nonresident workers may receive different withholding treatment if they provide the required documentation.

Employees working across other state borders should not assume that the same reciprocal treatment applies.

Remote work and employment across multiple jurisdictions can introduce additional tax considerations.

Consult the Minnesota Department of Revenue before applying an interstate withholding exemption.

## Planning Your Minnesota Monthly Budget

Use estimated take-home income rather than gross salary when establishing your household budget.

Account for housing, groceries, transportation, utilities, healthcare and required debt payments.

Employees living in Minnesota may also benefit from budgeting for seasonal heating expenses and winter-related transportation costs.

Compare employer retirement matching, insurance premiums and paid leave arrangements when evaluating job offers.

Our [emergency fund calculator](/savings/emergency-fund-calculator/) can help establish a suitable savings target, while our [salary-to-hourly calculator](/calculators/salary-to-hourly-calculator/) can help compare different compensation arrangements.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is Minnesota's income tax rate in 2026?

Minnesota uses progressive individual income tax rates of 5.35%, 6.80%, 7.85% and 9.85%. Actual paycheck withholding depends on taxable wages, applicable allowances and withholding classification.

### How much is deducted for Minnesota Paid Leave?

Employers may generally deduct up to 0.44% of covered employee wages in 2026. The applicable rounded annual contribution wage ceiling is $185,000.

### Why did my Minnesota take-home pay change in January 2026?

Minnesota introduced its Paid Leave program in January 2026. Updated federal and state withholding schedules, contribution limits and employee benefits can also affect paycheck amounts.
